title: Nataraja explained
hook: a flame held in the open palm, level with the drum on the other side: the beginning in one hand, the ending in the other

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the drum: the beat that starts the dance, and the sounds of a language in the story. Which rhythm did you notice? Today, the other hand, and the end of a week. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.
screen: `LANGUAGE BEGINS AS A BEAT.` · `TODAY: THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Birthday candles go out with a breath and a wish. A campfire burns down to embers while everyone's still talking. A match flares, does its one job, and is shaken out. Fire is the thing that's always ending. Now go back to Nataraja. Opposite the drum, in his upper left hand, held up in an open palm the way someone might carry a small lamp, is a flame. Not a torch, not a weapon. Just fire, resting in the hand.
screen: `CANDLES, EMBERS, A MATCH.` → `FIRE IS ALWAYS ENDING.` → `A FLAME IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading of the image, the flame is dissolution. Things are made, they last a while, and in the end they're taken apart and drawn back in. The fire in that hand is the ending. Now look at where the sculptor put it. The drum is on one side. The flame is on the other. Both are raised to the same height, both held lightly, balanced across the dancer's shoulders like the two pans of a scale. The beginning in one hand, the ending in the other, and neither one is higher than the other. Neither is dropped. That's the picture's quiet argument. Read this way, ending isn't the enemy of the dance. It's half of it. The fire clears the stage so the drum can start again. Remember who's holding it. Shiva is the one who dances in the cremation ground, smeared with ash, the groom whose looks made Mena faint. Ash is what fire leaves behind, and he wears it like clothing. Which brings us to the end of a week. It opened with Parvati's tapas and the visitor who turned out to be Shiva. Then the wedding, and a god who showed a gentler face. Three cities and one arrow. The lord who is half woman, and the close of the Shiva Purana. Then the dancer: the calm face, the drum, and now the flame. Every week ends. The flame in Nataraja's hand says that's not a failure of the week. It's how a new one gets room to start.
screen: `THE FLAME: THE ENDING.` · `DRUM AND FLAME AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `ENDING IS HALF THE DANCE.` · `A WEEK OF FIRE, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both. Settle, and let the breath slow. Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. Into the right palm, put something that's beginning in your life: a new job, a new friendship, a habit, a season. Into the left palm, put something that's ending, or needs to: a chapter, a role, a worry you've carried too long. Let both hands rest at the same height. Don't lift one and drop the other. Just breathe with both. If you pray, you can offer both to Shiva, or to God, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Nataraja explained. Today, the flame in his upper left hand: the ending, held level with the drum's beginning, both part of the same dance.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Today, finish one thing all the way, close the tab, file the paper, say the goodbye, before you start the next. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven. A week, kept.

howItsDone: In Nataraja images the upper left hand holds a flame, read as dissolution, balanced against the drum of creation in the upper right; devotees offer lamps before Nataraja in worship.

original.note: Sanskrit: agni, fire, the flame held in Nataraja's upper left hand.

trapdoor: what you thought: he's carrying a torch to see by.
what it means: the flame of dissolution, the ending, held level with the drum of beginning.
what a scholar hears: creation and dissolution balanced, two of the acts the dance is read as performing.

notes: Week end (1121–1127): the look-back lists 1121's tapas (written by another writer) and 1122–1127.

Reading the flame as dissolution (samhara) and the drum as creation (srishti) is the standard interpretation; 'the same height' describes the classic South Indian bronzes, though individual images vary. Confirm.
Shiva dancing in the cremation ground is a common Shaiva image; kept general.
The fuller list of the dance's acts is saved for day 1131; the trapdoor names only two.
